## What I found

**The framing in your brief — "which states have biometric laws" — turned out to be the wrong lens.** What
actually determines danger is whether a state combines a private right of action, statutory damages, no injury requirement, and plaintiff-side fee shifting. **Only Illinois has all four.**

Everything else is attorney-general enforcement: serious, but a compliance project rather than an existential one.

**Your four answers, briefly:**
- **Notice/consent:** build one flow to the Illinois BIPA §15(b) standard — standalone (never bundled with
ToS), stating purpose *and* length of term in writing, before the camera opens. That single flow satisfies all ~20 op

t-in states. The 2024 BIPA amendment expressly blessed electronic signatures, so no wet ink needed.
- **Retention:** Texas is the binding constraint at one

year after purpose expires, not Illinois' three years.
- **Private right of action:** Illinois (everything), Washington MHMD (via CPA), California (breach only).

Nowhere else.
- **Penalties:** $1,000/$5,000 per person in IL; $25,000/violation in TX; $20,000 in CO; $5,000–$10,000 el

sewhere.

**Three things I'd want you to read even if you skip the rest:**

1. **BIPA has no fraud-prevention exemption.** Someone will assume it does. The

closest case on record — Jumio/Binance — is your exact fact pattern and survived a motion to dismiss.

2. **Washington is inverted.** The dedicated biometric stat

ute probably doesn't reach you (photo-derived-data exclusion plus an express fraud-prevention carve-out). My Health My Data does, has **no size threshold whatsoever**, and has a private right of action.

3. **Your larg

est number isn't a consent statute — it's a breach.** California §1798.150 is $100–$750 per consumer with no proof of harm. Encryption is a statutory defence; not storing the template is better. That's an engineering ticket, not a legal sp

end.

I also checked and would ask you *not* to rely on the "we delete it instantly so it isn't collection" argument — §
15(b) attaches at capture, and *Zellmer v. Meta* is squarely distinguishable because our whole purpose is identification. Build zero-retention anyway, for six other reasons in the

report.

**Two flags on my own work:** at least one widely-circulated 50-state chart is wrong about Iowa and Utah (they're notice-plus-opt-out, not opt-in) — I corr

ected it against primary analyses, but spot-check any vendor chart you're handed. And three of my research subtasks are still showing open; the work is complete and in the report, but I lost their IDs mid-run and couldn't close them —

noted in the comment.

Nine subtasks are waiting on you, seven launch-blocking. The one that needs *you* specifically is the Illinois posture decision — com
ply, geo-defer, or offer a non-biometric path. I laid out all three with the tradeoffs rather than picking for you, since it's a ris
k-appetite call. I'd also add: exposure accrues from the first signup and the limitations period is five years, so "launch and fix it later" isn't one of the three
options.
